verses.text: So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.
Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself.
My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.

Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men's hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.
Brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another.
For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?
Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings. How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!
For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men.
We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored.
To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless.
We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it;
when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world.
I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.
Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
Therefore I urge you to imitate me.
That is why I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.
Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.
For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.
Which do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Sosthenes (1:1)
context.genre: Letter, answering reports and questions point by point
context.audience: The church in Corinth, founded by Paul a few years earlier
context.setting: Paul finishes his case about divisions. He asks the Corinthians to think of the apostles as servants and stewards, not stars. He contrasts their pride with the apostles’ hardships and calls them to imitate him, and he sends Timothy to remind them. He closes with a warning that he may come with a rod.
context.custom: A steward managed a household for the master and had to be trustworthy. The “spectacle” (v.9) pictures the end of a Roman triumph, when condemned prisoners were paraded and sent to die in the arena.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 5 turns from pride to a case of serious sin the church is proud of tolerating.
context.timelineBible: “Do not go beyond what is written” (v.6) probably refers to the Old Testament quotes in chapters 1-3. Paul’s “fools for Christ” echoes the suffering prophets.
context.sparkNotes: Paul says the apostles are servants and stewards, and only the Lord can judge. The Corinthians already feel rich and royal, but the apostles are hungry and homeless. Paul writes as a father, not to shame them, and sends Timothy. The kingdom is not talk but power.

translation.meaning: Managers of a household. The English “economy” comes from it.
Literally what is scraped off in cleaning. Paul says the apostles are treated as garbage.

otBackground.note: Do not boast in wisdom, but in knowing the Lord.
The “remnant” image behind Paul’s sense of the faithful.

overview.summary: Paul compares the Corinthians’ pride to the apostles’ hardships, urges them to imitate him as a spiritual father, and warns he will come to see their power, not their talk.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Ephesus to the church in Corinth.

history.t: A general’s parade ended with captives, some of whom were executed. Paul says the apostles are at the end of the line.
Paul’s young co-worker, who joined him in Acts 16, was sent ahead to Corinth.

customs.t: Often a trusted slave who ran the household. His job was faithfulness.
A disciplinary tool. A father might use it on a child.

archaeology.t: A large theater and an arena in Corinth show the entertainment world Paul alludes to.
Storage buildings near the harbor remind us how important Corinth’s trade was.

overview.discussion: Paul says the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. What is one area where my words are bigger than my life?
overview.book: The first letter to the Corinthians · 16 chapters. Paul’s answers to a lively and troubled church in a rich Greek port city.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: A carved relief of a gladiator found at Ephesus (Ephesus Museum, Turkey). Fights in the arena were a common public show in Roman cities. Paul says God has put the apostles on display "as men sentenced to death" (1 Corinthians 4:9) and speaks of fighting "beasts at Ephesus" (15:32).
